title: Salt in the Water
hookLine: a father drops salt into water overnight and tells his son, "you are that", and three great teachers hear it three ways
carry: tat tvam asi: three great readings, none ranked
tomorrow: a dead teacher's hand has three fingers folded. what did he leave undone?

lines: TAT TVAM ASI. YOU ARE THAT.
cards: Back to Shvetaketu and his father. Uddalaka hands him a lump of salt. Put this in a cup of water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning.
Next morning: give me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. It's gone.
Taste the water from the top. Salty. From the middle.

teach.b: Tat tvam asi is one of the most loved lines in Hinduism, and here's the teaching inside it: your atman, your deepest self, is not cut off from Brahman. But how?
Three of Vedanta's great teachers honor this same line and hear it differently.
Shankara reads it straight. You, at your deepest, are Brahman, not part of it. Advaita teachers use the space inside a clay pot: break the pot, and the space was never separate.

His school is Advaita, not-two. Ramanuja keeps the self real. In another Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of the one who dwells within all things, whose body they are, who guides them from inside.

teach.h: RAMANUJA: THE WORLD AS GOD'S BODY.
teach.b: So for Ramanuja, the world and every self are like Brahman's body: truly real, never apart. You are that, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it. His school is Vishishtadvaita.
Madhva hears difference. For him, the Lord, whom he knows as Vishnu, and the self are always two, and the self depends on him completely, like a reflection that's real only because something shines.
His school is Dvaita, two. Three readings, each argued from the same words, and Hindus in each line live and pray by them today. None is ranked here.
What all three share is the salt: the self is never on its own, outside the sacred.

how: Hindus in the Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita lines each study the Upanishads through their own teacher's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the line tat tvam asi is read and taught in each lineage in its own way.

o: one line that all teachers read in exactly one way
one line, you are that, heard three ways, none ranked
a single school that holds only Shankara's view

games.q: you are that, three ways — tap the pairs.
p: never two, like space in a pot
the world and selves as Brahman's body

s: all the great Vedanta teachers read tat tvam asi the same way
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each hear it differently, from the same texts.
for Ramanuja, the self is real and never apart from Brahman
like a body that truly belongs to the one who lives in it.
in the story, the salt is gone because the water washed it away
it can't be seen, but every sip tastes of it: that's Uddalaka's point.

games.q: a friend reads 'you are that' online and asks if Hindus think they're God. what's the honest answer?
o: yes, every Hindu believes exactly that.
it depends on the reading: not-two, God's body, or always two and close.
no, the line is only about salt.
games.why: Shankara hears identity, Ramanuja the self as Brahman's body, Madhva two who stay close. all three honor the line.

practice: Let the words come quietly, you are that. Hear them first as Shankara might, as open space no pot ever divided. Then as Ramanuja might, held from inside, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it.
Then as Madhva might, noticing you didn't make yourself shine. A few breaths each. You don't have to choose.
If you pray, you can let the line rest in the name you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Vedanta. Today, the line you are that, heard as not-two, as body and soul, and as two who stay close. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: you are that, from the Chandogya Upanishad, read differently by each Vedanta school.

carryVoice: Your line: tat tvam asi, three great readings, none ranked. Like salt in water, the self is never outside the sacred. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (the salt in water; tasting from top, middle and bottom; you are that)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7–6.16 (Uddalaka to Shvetaketu: the refrain, you are that)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the inner controller, whose body all things are)
